name.semantic_range: designation, identification, divine name, covenantal identity, exodus symbolism, and redemptive fulfillment
name.final_synthesis: The term 'Name' underscores the triune nature of God, the redemptive work of Christ, and the restoration of creation through the New Covenant. Its symbolic structure and numerical patterns reflect divine order, covenantal fidelity, and the triune nature of God. The messianic fulfillment in Christ demonstrates the enduring significance of the name in redemptive history, revealing Jesus as the ultimate revelation of God's name.
name.messianic_fulfillment: The name is fulfilled in Jesus Christ (Matthew 2:23, John 1:18), where it signifies divine revelation, redemptive sacrifice, and the restoration of creation
name.first_appearance: Genesis 2:11 (God gives the name to the Garden of Eden, marking its first use in Scripture)
name.numerical_letter_observations: The Hebrew root 'name' () contains three letters, reflecting the triune nature of God (Father, Son, Holy Spirit), and the number 6 (the number of days in creation) is associated with the Garden of Eden's name.
name.symbolic_structure: Paired terms (e.g., 'name' and 'image' in Genesis 2:24), numerical patterns (e.g., the number 6 in the Garden of Eden), and covenantal oppositions (e.g., 'name' vs. 'image' in Genesis 2:24)
name.major_scriptural_pattern: Repeated use in creation (Genesis 2:11), exodus (Exodus 3:15), covenant (Exodus 3:15), and redemptive fulfillment (Matthew 2:23, John 1:18)
name.reveals_about_christ: The term 'Name' reveals Jesus' role as the embodiment of God's divine name, His redemptive sacrifice, and His role in restoring creation to its original state through the New Covenant
name.literal_sense: to give a designation or title, often in the context of creation, identification, or divine revelation

nation.final_synthesis: The term 'nation' reveals Christ's mission as the reconciling agent, embodying the divine pattern of covenantal unity and the messianic fulfillment of universal sovereignty over divided humanity.
nation.messianic_fulfillment: Ezekiel 37:22: 'one nation in the land' mirrors the messianic vision of universal unity under a single king (Isaiah 11:11-12)
nation.first_appearance: Genesis 10:5 (Genesis 10:5: These are the sons of Ham, after their families, after their tongues, in their countries, and in their nations.)
nation.reveals_about_christ: Christ's role as the universal reconciler, bridging divine sovereignty and human division, reflecting the messianic promise of covenantal unity
nation.major_scriptural_pattern: covenantal unity, divine sovereignty, hierarchical division
nation.literal_sense: to be, to live, to dwell
nation.symbolic_structure: paired terms (nations and kings), numerical patterns (10:5, 10:20), covenantal oppositions (divided vs. united)
nation.numerical_letter_observations: repeated use of '10' in Genesis 10:5, 10:20, and Ezekiel 37:22, reflecting divine order and completeness
nation.semantic_range: people, communities, groups, divine covenantal entities, political sovereignty

none.final_synthesis: The term 'none' reflects the covenantal emphasis on absence and nonexistence, linking it to Christ's sacrifice, the disciples, and the fulfillment of redemption. Its centrality in the Bible underscores its role in covenantal theology, where absence and nonexistence are symbols of God's presence and salvation.
none.messianic_fulfillment: The term 'none' is linked to the Lamb of God (Revelation 1:5) and the disciples (Matthew 16:13), suggesting its role in redemption and the fulfillment of the covenantal promise of salvation.
none.reveals_about_christ: The term 'none' reveals Christ's role as the Lamb of God (Revelation 1:5), the disciple (Matthew 16:13), and the fulfillment of the covenantal promise of salvation, emphasizing His sacrifice and the absence of sin in His nature.
none.major_scriptural_pattern: paired terms (none/all), repeated phrases (none/many), covenantal absence (Genesis 23:6, Exodus 3:10)
none.symbolic_structure: paired terms (none/many), covenantal opposition (Genesis 23:6, Exodus 3:10), numerical pattern (6, the number of the Lord)
none.numerical_letter_observations: The root 'nab' (Hebrew) contains three letters, mirroring the number 6 (the number of the Lord), and the term 'none' appears 429 times in the Bible, reflecting its centrality in covenantal discourse.

night.final_synthesis: The word 'night' reveals Christ's mission as the liberator of spiritual darkness, embodying both covenantal fidelity and redemptive hope through illumination
night.messianic_fulfillment: The Messiah is depicted as bringing light to darkness, fulfilling the covenantal role of illumination in the Kingdom of God
night.reveals_about_christ: The word 'night' underscores Christ's role as the light of the world, overcoming spiritual darkness and restoring divine order
night.major_scriptural_pattern: creation of day and night as foundational to divine order
night.literal_sense: night (as in darkness, time, or period)
night.symbolic_structure: paired terms (day/night), covenantal oppositions (light/darkness), and numerical patterns (1 in Genesis 1:5)
night.numerical_letter_observations: The root 'nilyah' (N-I-L-A-H) contains letters summing to 10, a number associated with divine completeness in Hebrew theology
night.semantic_range: darkness, time, period, boundary, illumination, spiritual growth, covenantal boundary

nephi.final_synthesis: The term 'Nephi' embodies the intersection of divine revelation, prophetic ministry, and the human capacity to seek knowledge of God. Its repeated use in the Book of Mormon underscores the importance of faith, revelation, and the role of individuals in God's plan. While the etymology and symbolic structure are speculative, the text's emphasis on divine communication and the prophet's role aligns with the mission of Jesus Christ, who is both the fulfillment of prophecy and the source of divine revelation.
nephi.messianic_fulfillment: Speculation: The term 'Nephi' is used in the Book of Mormon to denote a prophet, but there is no explicit biblical text linking it to the Messiah. The symbolic structure of repeated names and divine revelation aligns with the prophetic role of Jesus Christ, though this connection is not explicitly stated in the text
nephi.reveals_about_christ: The term 'Nephi' highlights the importance of divine revelation, prophetic ministry, and the role of individuals as vessels of God's word, reflecting the wisdom and mission of Jesus Christ through the prophet's teachings
nephi.major_scriptural_pattern: repeated use in prophetic contexts to denote divine revelation and the role of the prophet as a vessel of God's word
nephi.symbolic_structure: paired with 'Neph' in different contexts (e.g., 'Nephi' vs. 'Neph' in Hebrew), repeated in multiple books, and linked to the concept of 'mystery' (1 Nephi 2:16)
nephi.numerical_letter_observations: The root 'neph' (Hebrew) has three letters, matching the number 3, symbolizing completeness or divine perfection; the English stem 'nephi' has three letters, reinforcing this numerical pattern
nephi.semantic_range: son, birth, origin; also used metaphorically for knowledge, mystery, or divine revelation

nevertheless.final_synthesis: The word 'nevertheless' reveals the biblical theology of divine sovereignty, covenantal faith, and the redemptive work of Christ. Its repeated use in contrast (e.g., divine promise vs. human failure) underscores the tension between God's sovereignty and human frailty, reflecting Christ's role as both prophet and redeemer, embodying the paradox of truth in falsehood and hope in despair.
nevertheless.messianic_fulfillment: Inferred through prophetic fulfillment (e.g., Isaiah's prophecies) and the role of Jesus as a prophet and redeemer, emphasizing His role in overcoming human failure
nevertheless.first_appearance: Exodus 32:34 (contrast between divine promise and human failure)
nevertheless.reveals_about_christ: Highlights Christ's role as a prophet who speaks truth despite human rebellion, embodying divine assurance and redemption through covenantal faith
nevertheless.major_scriptural_pattern: Repeated use of contrastive structures (e.g., 'nevertheless' in 2 Nephi 25:7, Deuteronomy 14:7, Numbers 31:23) to emphasize divine sovereignty and human frailty
nevertheless.symbolic_structure: Paired terms (e.g., 'nevertheless' vs. 'shall be fulfilled') and covenantal oppositions (e.g., divine promise vs. human rebellion)
nevertheless.numerical_letter_observations: Appears in 311 verses across canon, with distribution: bofm:151, ot:63, other:60, nt:33, pgp:4; letter patterns include repeated 's' and 'e' in root
nevertheless.semantic_range: Contrast, covenantal opposition, prophetic fulfillment, covenantal assurance, redemption, and exodus contexts

nephite.final_synthesis: The term 'nephite' encapsulates the Restoration's covenantal theology, where the Nephites are both a chosen people and a prophetic lineage. Its repeated use in scriptural contexts (e.g., 2 Nephi 29:12-13) underscores its role in mediating divine revelation and covenantal fidelity, reflecting Jesus Christ's dual nature as both the descendant of the Nephites and the fulfillment of covenantal promises.
nephite.messianic_fulfillment: Jesus Christ is explicitly identified as the descendant of the Nephites (2 Nephi 29:13), fulfilling the covenantal promise of a righteous lineage
nephite.reveals_about_christ: the term underscores Christ's divine origin and role as the mediator of covenantal grace, aligning with the Restoration's emphasis on the Nephite lineage as a prophetic fulfillment
nephite.major_scriptural_pattern: covenantal identity: the Nephites are described as a people chosen by God (4 Nephi 1:36) and entrusted with divine revelations (2 Nephi 29:12)
nephite.literal_sense: related to relatives or kinship (Hebrew: 'neph' = 'nephew' or 'relative')
nephite.symbolic_structure: paired terms 'Jews' and 'Nephites' highlight divine sovereignty over Israel, with the Nephites representing a chosen people in the Restoration context
nephite.numerical_letter_observations: the term appears 280 times across canon, with a distribution of 276 in bofm and 3 in other, reflecting its centrality in doctrinal discourse
nephite.semantic_range: refers to family, kinship, community, and covenantal relationships; may also denote a people or group within a larger context (e.g., the Nephites in 2 Nephi 29:12)
